source.title: Chemical reasoning in LLMs unlocks strategy-aware synthesis planning and reaction mechanism elucidation
source.authors: A. Bran; Théo A. Neukomm; Daniel P. Armstrong; Zlatko Joncev; P. Schwaller

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the paper and supplementary information are included.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares language-model performance on chemistry tasks and explicitly relates capability to model size and model generation. It does not measure held-out language-model loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and discusses scaling as background, but those cited results are not this study's results. Its own chemistry-task performance comparisons bear on V6, not on loss power laws, extrapolation of loss, compute-optimal allocation, architecture-shape effects, other-modality loss scaling, or scaling-law fit dependence. Mechanism benchmark figures and the strategy-planning benchmark provide additional downstream-task evaluations, but the reported scaling-related outcomes are qualitative rather than loss-versus-size measurements.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks commercial and open LLMs on chemistry tasks: correlation with scripted ground truth for route scoring, and score gaps and top-1 accuracy for mechanism steps. It reports no parameter counts, tokens, compute or pretraining loss, and fits no curve, so performance is never measured against a scale variable. Its statement that performance scales strongly with model size is a qualitative reading of a model ranking. The models differ in size, generation, provider and post-training (e.g. reasoning-trained, distilled) all at once. It cites Kaplan et al. as background. The results cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss, so it does not test V6 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right but misses the main point. The authors chiefly conclude that LLMs used as evaluators inside traditional search (Synthegy) enable strategy-aware retrosynthesis and mechanism elucidation. Separately, they say newer and larger models show stronger chemical reasoning, with smaller models near random. They interpret the latter as a capability threshold, not a measured scaling law. They give no parameter counts or losses.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates chemistry-task performance across language models; it does not sweep training parameters, tokens, or compute, and does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported capability depends on task difficulty: the best models perform better on simple mechanism tasks than on more complex ones. The strategy-planning text also notes that differences may reflect tokenization and prompting strategies, but does not isolate those factors experimentally as scaling-law fit choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Across unsized commercial and open LLMs, chemistry-task performance rises with model generation and apparent size. Smaller or distilled variants (4o-mini, DeepSeek-r1 distills, o4-mini, most Llama models) perform near random or poorly. The authors read this as a threshold beyond which capability appears, not a smooth trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream chemical-reasoning capability of LLMs appears only above a model-size or generation threshold (emergence-style), judged from model rankings without measured scale.

record.problems: The study does not report model parameter counts or pretraining losses alongside the downstream results, and does not fit a quantitative performance-versus-scale relationship. Some qualitative comparisons refer to model groups or an unnamed best-performing model. Reported chemistry-task performance is task-dependent.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports detailed strategy-planning benchmark plots and mechanism top-1 accuracies by model and task, including Table 1 values and supplementary figures. Those results are downstream task evaluations, but they do not provide parameter counts or pretraining loss and do not measure a scaling curve; only the explicit qualitative outcomes relevant to the stated model-scale comparison are retained here.

untested.parts: No loss scaling in other regimes.
Downstream performance versus parameters, compute or pretraining loss, and whether it is predictable. Model sizes are not stated and no curve is fitted.

missing.what: Within-family size contrast: GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-4o top-1 accuracy per mechanism task. 4o-mini is lower on most tasks (e.g. task 8: 5 vs 18), random baseline 17%. No parameter counts given.
missing.versions: none (closest to V6, but no scale variable)

missing.what: Distilled DeepSeek-r1 and o4-mini underperform their larger counterparts on the strategy benchmark; Llama family results shown.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2' is overturned. The models' sizes are unknown and confounded with generation, provider and reasoning post-training, so the size statements are qualitative rankings. The study is a chemistry application paper and is not an original source of any version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out cross-entropy loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run held-out loss from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations, and their dependence on compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.

The study compares downstream chemistry-task performance across models, but does not measure performance as a function of stated parameter counts or pretraining loss, nor fit a predictive scaling curve.
Scaling-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, fitting choices, and systematic departures from power-law curves.

rows.subject: Smaller models (not individually specified)
rows.size_stated: smaller models; parameter counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated on the strategy-aware synthesis-planning benchmark; the text summarizes performance by model size.
rows.value: Performance was indistinguishable from random choice, even for short routes.
rows.note: Qualitative summary for smaller models as a group; no individual model results or parameter counts are given in this statement.
rows.check: Unnamed 'smaller models' of unstated size, at random-choice level, with the detail in an unresolved SI reference. This is a group-level threshold remark, not performance against a measured scale, so it cannot bear on predictable scaling.

rows.subject: gemini-2.5-pro
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated on the strategy-aware synthesis-planning benchmark.
rows.measure: Correlation of model-produced scores with benchmark ground-truth scores
rows.value: Improved by over 50% relative to the next-best model.
rows.note: The text reports the relative improvement but not the underlying score in this statement.
rows.check: Gemini-2.5-pro beats the next-best model by over 50% (Fig 2c, performance over release time). This compares models across release dates and providers with unknown sizes; it is a capability-over-time ranking, not a scale measure.

rows.subject: Best-performing model (not identified in this statement)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated model ability to score correct versus alternative moves in the mechanism-elucidation benchmark.
rows.measure: Separation of ground-truth mechanism moves from alternatives
rows.baseline: alternative moves; numeric baseline not stated for this measure
rows.value: Close to perfect performance on simple reactions.
rows.note: The model is not named in the text description of this outcome.
rows.check: The best model is near-perfect on simple mechanism tasks. This is a task-difficulty comparison within one model, not a scale relation.

rows.subject: Best-performing model (not identified in this statement)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated model ability to score correct versus alternative moves in the mechanism-elucidation benchmark.

conditions.value: more complex reactions, including Michael additions on larger molecules and miscellaneous reactions

rows.measure: Separation of ground-truth mechanism moves from alternatives
rows.baseline: alternative moves; numeric baseline not stated for this measure
rows.value: Performance was poorer than on simple reactions, although the best models could still distinguish good moves from incorrect alternatives.
rows.note: The text describes a task-dependent decline rather than a loss-scaling result.
rows.check: Lower performance on complex mechanisms is a task-difficulty effect, not scale.

rows.subject: GPT-4o-mini
rows.measure: Ability to distinguish correct mechanism moves from alternatives
rows.value: Generally performed badly, including on the simplest tasks.
rows.note: The study does not give a parameter count in this statement.
rows.check: GPT-4o-mini performs poorly, but no size is given. Table 1 gives 4o-mini below 4o on most tasks, which is the only within-family size contrast. With two unsized points there is no predictability test.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported model-size and model-generation comparisons on chemistry tasks
reader_labels.reason: The authors report stronger performance for larger/newer models, including a greater-than-50% relative improvement by gemini-2.5-pro over the next-best model on the strategy-planning benchmark (R2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across model groups and mechanism-task difficulty
reader_labels.reason: Smaller models could be at random-choice performance, GPT-4o-mini performed poorly, and even the best models did worse on complex mechanisms; the study does not establish a general predictive relationship to parameter count or pretraining loss (R1, R3, R4, R5).
